description: We are an ambitious team participating in NASA Space Apps Cairo, bringing together creative minds passionate about space, science, and technology. We value teamwork, innovation, and problem-solving. We are looking for motivated members skilled in programming, AI, research, astronomy, data analysis, design, and communication. Most importantly, we welcome curious people who are eager to learn, share ideas, and turn challenges into innovative solutions. 🚀
summary:
We developed CAVE-SIGHT, an open-data screening pipeline and interactive web platform that ranks Earth locations as analogs for permanent Moon bases, with a planned extension to Mars.

It addresses the challenge by anchoring on two 2024 discoveries: a ~45 m subsurface conduit beneath the Moon’s Mare Tranquillitatis Pit (Carrer & Bruzzone) and the 45 m wide Umm Jirsan lava tube in Saudi Arabia (Stewart et al.). For eight global sites, CAVE-SIGHT combines NASA POWER climate data with SRTM elevation models and ranks them without manual feature weights. Umm Jirsan ranked first, and all five volcanic candidates outranked both sand-dune negative controls. Interactive maps, radar-chart comparisons and a transparent scoring method show where each site matches and where it differs.

This matters because long-term habitats need shielding from radiation, micrometeorites and extreme thermal swings, which basaltic lava tubes can provide. CAVE-SIGHT gives researchers a reproducible, uncertainty-aware way to select terrestrial testbeds and prioritize subsurface habitat studies.
details:
CAVE-SIGHT is a two-part system: a data pipeline and an interactive web platform.

The pipeline ingests eight global coordinates: five volcanic lava-tube fields (Umm Jirsan in Saudi Arabia, El Pinacate in Mexico, Cima, Lava Beds, and Craters of the Moon in the USA, Undara in Australia) and two non-volcanic sand-dune fields as negative controls (Algodones, Simpson Desert). For each site it queries live NASA POWER climatology (surface albedo, diurnal temperature range, precipitation, solar irradiance, mean temperature) and extracts a 3×3 SRTM digital elevation window to characterize local terrain. A transparent, weight-free mathematical model then ranks all sites against lunar reference conditions. The method is anchored on two 2024 discoveries: the ~45 m subsurface conduit detected beneath the Moon’s Mare Tranquillitatis Pit (Carrer & Bruzzone, 2024) and the 45 m wide Umm Jirsan lava tube (Stewart et al., 2024), a matching Earth–Moon conduit scale that serves as our reference point.

The web platform presents the results through five modules: a scientific synthesis banner, a dual-planet split view (Earth satellite/topographic maps beside NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek), a 5-axis radar-chart inspector for per-site comparison, a filterable site registry with a live screening calculator, and a Phase 2 roadmap covering Mars skylights (Arsia Mons, Olympus Mons), EMIT hyperspectral mineralogy, and roof-stability modeling across gravity regimes.

Results: Umm Jirsan ranked first without any manual feature weighting, and all five volcanic candidates outranked both sand-dune controls, evidence that the screening separates genuine lava-tube terrain from superficially similar arid landscapes.

Benefits and intended impact: Analog site selection today is often qualitative and scattered across papers. CAVE-SIGHT turns it into a reproducible, auditable screening step: every input is open data, every score is traceable to a formula, and uncertainties and limitations are stated rather than hidden behind a single similarity number. The intended impact is a decision-support tool that helps researchers and mission planners shortlist terrestrial testbeds for subsurface habitat studies, the lava tubes that could shield future crews from cosmic radiation, micrometeorites, and extreme thermal swings.

Tools and technologies:

  • Data: NASA POWER API (climatology), SRTM elevation via the Open-Meteo Elevation API, Esri World Imagery/Topo tiles, NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek; peer-reviewed 2024 radar and field studies.
  • Pipeline: Python in Google Colab (requests, pandas, NumPy, SciPy for the Mann-Whitney U test), outputting CSV/JSON.
  • Platform: a standalone HTML/CSS/JavaScript website (Leaflet maps, Chart.js radar charts), deployed free on Vercel with no backend and no API keys, fully reproducible by anyone.

Creativity and considerations: The creative core is the Earth–Moon calibration idea: using the coincidence of two independently measured 45 m conduits, published the same year, to anchor an analog-screening method. We also deliberately included negative-control sites, rare in analog studies, so the model must prove it rejects false positives, not just confirm favorites. Key factors we considered: scientific honesty (no arbitrary weights, stated uncertainties, small-sample statistics reported with care), accessibility (free, open data; runs in a browser), and extensibility (the same pipeline generalizes to Mars candidates in Phase 2).
